name: Subhuman / LTN / HTN / Chad tiers

card.summary: The ranking vocabulary of looksmaxxing: from subhuman through LTN and HTN to Chad, descended from the PSL scale.
card.note: Researchers consider parts of the PSL system pseudoscientific; critics object to dehumanising labels.

quick.overview:
Tier language ranks men by perceived looks. The bottom is 'subhuman', the middle splits into low-tier and high-tier normie, and the top is Chad, with further steps like giga Chad.

The system descends from the PSL scale, which scores facial attractiveness from 1 to 8.
quick.mechanism: It is a shared vocabulary, not a procedure. Members rate faces against the scale, often in forum photo threads.
quick.risks: Critics note the labels can be dehumanising and that the scale has no scientific validation; effects on self-image have not been formally studied in the sources reviewed.

lead: Subhuman, LTN (low-tier normie), HTN (high-tier normie) and Chad are the rungs of a tier vocabulary used in looksmaxxing communities to place a man's looks on a ladder. The point of the ladder, for the people who use it, is orientation: knowing roughly where one's face sits tells a person how far there is to go and which improvements, such as skin, body fat, grooming, hair or facial structure, might move them up.[1]

The system descends from the PSL (Perceived Sexual Levels) scale, which rates facial attractiveness from 1 to 8 and was designed around how its authors believed women perceive men.[1] Wikipedia lists seven categories: subhuman or sub-3, low-tier normie, mid-tier normie, high-tier normie, Chadlite, Chad and giga Chad.[1] A simpler three-tier version associated with the streamer Clavicular uses subhuman, normie and Chad.[1]
Researchers and critics describe parts of the scale as pseudoscientific, and some commentators object to the label 'subhuman' itself.[1] No studies have tested the tier system as a measurement tool.

chain: Place one's face on the tier ladder
Identify which traits hold the rating down
Work on those traits (skin, leanness, grooming, hair, structure)
angle.text: Community members use the tiers as a shorthand for where they stand and how far a given change might move them, for example from low-tier to high-tier normie. The vocabulary organises improvement goals; it does not itself change anyone's appearance.

infobox: Subhuman, LTN, MTN, HTN, Chadlite, Chad, giga Chad[1]

paras: Subhuman (or sub-3) is the lowest PSL category. Low-tier, mid-tier and high-tier normie cover the middle of the range, where most people are placed, and Chadlite, Chad and giga Chad describe progressively more attractive men.[1] Chad is manosphere slang for an attractive, sexually successful man, and Stacy and Becky are the corresponding terms for women.[2] Abbreviations such as LTN and HTN are community shorthand; Wikipedia spells out the underlying categories rather than using the abbreviations.[1]

Members often add a letter for the specifics, so that discussions of a single face mention 'HTN' or 'LTN' alongside observations about the eyes, jaw or skin. On looksmax.org, posts titled around moving between tiers, such as a before-and-after photo comparison across puberty, show the labels being used to describe change over time.[3]

Looksmaxxing appeared on incel and manosphere message boards in the 2010s, where discussion credited sexual success to the genetic advantages of 'Chads'.[1] The rating vocabulary came out of the three PSL forums, PUAHate.com, Sluthate.com and Lookism.net, whose community was tied to black pill ideas; those forums are now defunct.[1] TikTok carried the language to wider audiences in the early 2020s, often in a self-improvement or self-deprecating register.[1] Later coverage tied the terms to streamers such as Clavicular, and tech coverage in 2025 reported on a chatbot that used the word 'subhuman' when discussing surgeries.[1][4]

Writer Becca Rothfeld criticised, in The New Yorker in March 2026, the practice of labelling people subhuman, along with racist language used by some participants.[1] Wikipedia describes the PSL scale as regarded by critics as pseudoscientific, noting that it rates only the face and encodes assumed female preferences.[1] Commentators have linked looksmaxxing culture to incel subculture, and a 2025 study by Halpin and colleagues argued that it promotes a hegemonic masculine gaze on male bodies.[1] Some participants report benefits such as peer affirmation, though the article notes this is often mixed with critique.[1]

timeline.event: Looksmaxxing appears on incel message boards; PSL forums develop the rating vocabulary.[1]
TikTok spreads looksmaxxing language to wider audiences.[1]
Commentary links TikTok looksmaxxing content to incel-adjacent views.[1]
The New Yorker publishes Rothfeld's critique of the 'subhuman' label.[1]

lore.intro: Members use tier labels in photo-rating threads and in discussions of whether a given change can move someone up a tier.[3]

claims.claim: A man's face fits a fixed tier that predicts how women respond
claims.believers: Proponents say the PSL scale reflects how women perceive men and that tier determines dating outcomes.[1]
claims.experts: Researchers and critics describe parts of the scale as pseudoscientific and note it rates only the face.[1]

claims.claim: Tiers can change through self-improvement and maturation
claims.believers: Users post before-and-after comparisons, including puberty changes, to show movement such as subhuman to LTN.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes surgeons and doctors consider some looksmaxxing methods risky; no study has tested tier movement.[1]
